newsitem.title: POLAND: Flood boosts poll lead of Polish right to 11 pct.
newsitem.headline: Flood boosts poll lead of Polish right to 11 pct.

text.p: Poland's Solidarity-led opposition has widened its lead over the ruling coalition after weeks of disastrous flooding, an independent opinion poll showed on Tuesday.
The PBS survey, conducted nine weeks ahead of parliamentary elections on September 21, showed the potential opposition coalition's lead over the government had widened to 11 percentage points.
This was an increase of almost five percentage points from the previous poll, held before some of the worst floods for centuries hit Poland earlier in July.

The opposition heavily criticised the government for its handling of the flooding, which has killed 55 people, forced tens of thousands from their homes and caused damage running into billions of dollars.

"The floods in southern Poland had a decisive influence on the change in voter preferences and offset the earlier negative perceptions of the AWS (Solidarity) from infighting within that group," said Ryszard Gudyka, analyst at PBS (Social Research Workshop).

Presented with a number of potential coalitions, 20 percent of Poles favoured an opposition grouping comprising the right-wing Solidarity Election Action (AWS), Movement for Reconstruction of Poland (ROP) and centrist Union for Freedom (UW), the survey carried out on July 19-20 showed.
This was up from 18.7 percent in a previous PBS survey in June.
The ruling coalition of the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and Peasant Party (PSL) got nine percent of preferences in the July survey, versus 12.4 percent in June.

An alternative potential coalition of the ruling SLD, with the opposition Union for Freedom and the Labour Union (UP), was shown to be a much stronger contender than the current ruling combination, and to have made marginal gains since June.
The number of Poles who would like to see such a team in power rose to 18 percent from 17.8 percent in June.
PBS also asked Poles who they expected, irrespective of their preferences, was most likely to win the elections and the results showed most people still expected the ruling coalition to win.
